setup: A Treasury bond issued on 1 March trades special at a 0.25% annual spread (actual/360). It is expected to go back to general collateral rates after 30 June, so the special lasts 122 days. A dealer lends USD 100 of cash against it.
ask: The financing value of lending the USD 100 is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.0085
options.why: Dropped a zero from the spread (0.25% treated as 0.025%), a decimal slip that shrinks the answer 10 times.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.25
options.why: Took the full-year spread and left out the day fraction $122/360$.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.85
options.why: Divided the days by 36 instead of 360, so the value is 10 times too big.

takeaway: A special spread earns only for the days it lasts: annual spread times days/360. Here about a third of a year, so about a third of 25 cents.

setup: A bond issued on 31 March trades special at a 0.30% spread until 30 September, then at GC. Value per USD 100 is $100 \times 0.0030 \times \text{days}/360$ (actual/360). April to September have 30, 31, 30, 31, 31 and 30 days.
ask: The day-count fraction $\text{days}/360$ for the special period is:

options.label: Exactly 0.50
options.why: Treated six months as 6 × 30 = 180 days. Actual/360 counts the real days, and four of these months have 31.

options.label: Below 0.50
options.why: Six months can never be fewer than 180 days, since every month has at least 30. The four 31-day months push the count to 183.

takeaway: Under actual/360 a six-month window with four 31-day months is slightly more than half a 'year', so the value runs a touch above half the annual spread.

setup: Lending USD 200 of cash at a 0.25% spread for 150 days is valued as $200 \times 0.0025 \times 150/360 = 0.208$ (USD) under actual/360. A colleague re-prices the same trade on an actual/365 basis.
ask: Compared with USD 0.208, the actual/365 value is:

options.label: Slightly higher
options.why: Read the 365 as adding days. The days stay at 150; a bigger denominator shrinks the fraction ($150/365 = 0.411$ against $0.417$).

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The convention changes the denominator, so $150/D$ changes. The gap is small (about 1.4%) but it is not zero.

takeaway: A larger day-count denominator means a smaller accrual fraction, so actual/365 gives a slightly lower value than actual/360.

reading: LTR-14: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
setup: A USD 20m credit line has USD 6m drawn, with a 65% chance the customer draws the rest. The liquidity cushion is funded at a 3-year term, so its cost is that term's liquidity premium. Premiums for terms of 1 to 5 years are 5, 9, 15, 25 and 40 bps; average cost of funds is 8 bps flat. Charge = (undrawn/limit) × probability × cushion cost, applied to the USD 20m limit.
ask: The dollar charge for contingent liquidity risk is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 1,400
options.why: Read the 15 bps as 1.5 bps (decimal slip), which shrinks the charge 10 times.

options.label: ≈ USD 4,550
options.why: Picked the 1-year premium (5 bps) instead of the 3-year point (15 bps).

options.label: ≈ USD 36,400
options.why: Picked the 5-year premium (40 bps) instead of the 3-year point (15 bps).

takeaway: Read the premium at the term the cushion actually funds. The expected drawdown is 0.70 × 0.65 of the limit, so the rate is under half the 15 bps cost.

reading: LTR-14: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
setup: A committed line has a USD 40m limit with USD 15m drawn. The bank puts a 40% probability on the client drawing all of the remaining commitment, and the cushion costs 25 bps. The charge is quoted as a rate on the whole USD 40m limit: (undrawn/limit) × probability × cushion cost. Quoted per dollar of undrawn commitment instead, it would be $0.40 \times 25 = 10$ bps.
ask: The rate quoted on the limit is:

options.label: Equal to 10 bps
options.why: That is the rate per dollar of undrawn commitment. Spreading the same dollar cost over the full limit scales it by the undrawn fraction.

options.label: Above 10 bps
options.why: Inverted the undrawn fraction (limit/undrawn = 1.6, giving 16 bps). The limit is larger than the undrawn amount, so the rate on it is smaller.

takeaway: Rate on the limit = rate on the undrawn amount × undrawn fraction, so it is always below the per-undrawn figure unless nothing is drawn.

reading: LTR-14: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
setup: A credit line has a USD 120m limit with USD 56m drawn. Customer K has a 75% probability of drawing the remainder, and the cushion costs 32 bps. The rate is (undrawn/limit) × probability × 32 bps, so two factors below 1 scale the 32 bps down.
ask: Which factor cuts the 32 bps cost by more?

options.label: The drawdown probability, 75%
options.why: Compared the 75% with 1 and stopped; the undrawn fraction is only 0.533, which is further below 1 than 0.75.

options.label: They cut it equally
options.why: Both are fractions, but not the same size: 0.533 against 0.75.

takeaway: In a product of fractions the smaller one cuts more. Check both factors before assuming the probability is the main discount.
